title: The Levite's Concubine and the Crime at Gibeah
summary: A Levite from Ephraim goes to Bethlehem to bring back his concubine, lingers through days of hospitality from her father, and sets out late. Refusing to stop in Jebus, a non-Israelite city, he spends the night in the Benjamite town of Gibeah, where only an old man takes them in. Men of the city surround the house, the Levite pushes his concubine out to them, and she is abused through the night and found dead at the door; the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
story: This is the second story of the epilogue, and it is the darkest chapter in the book, perhaps in the whole Old Testament. The first story (chapters 17-18) showed the corruption of Israel's worship; this one shows the corruption of its moral and social life. It begins with the same refrain, that there was no king in Israel, and with another Levite connected to Bethlehem and the hill country of Ephraim. The story deliberately echoes Genesis 19, where the men of Sodom surround Lot's house. The point is devastating: an Israelite town now behaves like Sodom. The Levite's grisly summons will set in motion the civil war of chapters 20-21.
historical:
The route runs from Bethlehem north toward the hill country of Ephraim. Jebus, the name here for Jerusalem, was still held by the Jebusites; it would not be taken until David captured it (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Gibeah, a few miles north of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, is usually identified with Tell el-Ful. Ramah was a little further north. Gibeah later became the hometown and capital of Saul, Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:26), and many interpreters think the story's harsh picture of Gibeah reflects the rivalry between Saul's house and David's.

The prophet Hosea, centuries later, remembered this event as a byword for deep corruption, speaking of the days of Gibeah (Hosea 9:9; 10:9). Chapter 20's mention of Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, suggests that these events happened early in the period of the judges, within a generation or two of the entry into Canaan, which makes the depth of the corruption all the more striking.
cultural:
A concubine was a secondary wife, legally bound to a man but without the full status of a primary wife, often from a poorer family. The Hebrew says she was unfaithful to him; the ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) and some interpreters read that she became angry with him, which may fit better with her returning to her father's house. Either way, the Levite goes after her to speak kindly to her, literally to speak to her heart, a phrase used elsewhere for comfort and reconciliation.

Hospitality was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East. Travelers depended on it, and a host was bound to protect guests under his roof. The father's repeated insistence that the Levite stay reflects that duty, perhaps pressed to excess. In Gibeah, the absence of hospitality from anyone but an outsider from Ephraim is a sign of the town's corruption. The old man's offer of his own daughter and the concubine reflects a culture in which the protection of a male guest was ranked above the safety of women, a hierarchy the narrative exposes in all its horror. Cutting up an animal and sending the pieces as a summons to war appears again in 1 Samuel 11:7, when Saul does the same with oxen; the Levite does it with a woman.
literary: The chapter is built in two halves. The first (19:1-9) is slow and repetitive: the father detains the Levite day after day with food, drink, and invitations to stay. The pace is almost comic, but it has a purpose, creating the late departure that leads to disaster. The second half (19:10-30) moves steadily toward catastrophe. The Levite refuses to stay among foreigners, choosing an Israelite town for safety, and finds no safety there. The echoes of Genesis 19 are deliberate: a visitor taken in by a sojourner, men surrounding the house and demanding the guest, the host offering women instead. In Genesis the angels rescue those inside; here no one intervenes. The narrator's description of the woman with her hands on the threshold (19:27) is one of the most painful images in Scripture, and the Levite's words to her, “Get up,” and “Let us go” (19:28), show his coldness. The chapter ends with Israel's shocked response and a call to consider, take counsel, and speak.

doctrines.note: The chapter shows sin at its most brutal: sexual violence, betrayal by the one who should protect, and a town without justice. The comparison with Sodom shows that the covenant people had become like the nations God had judged.

The woman is never named and never speaks. The narrative forces the reader to see her suffering and to recognize that she, too, bore God's image. Her treatment exposes the failure of those around her.
The Levite's summons demands a response from all Israel, and the people's words call for moral reckoning. The chapter sets up the question of how a holy people should respond to such evil.

words.note: Pilegesh, concubine, a wife of secondary status. The word appears eight times in this chapter, always without her name. Her status made her vulnerable, and the story shows how that vulnerability was exploited by her husband, her host, and the men of the city.

Nevalah, folly, disgrace, or outrage, used by the old man in 19:23-24. In the Old Testament the word describes shocking acts that violate the covenant's moral order, especially sexual crimes (Genesis 34:7; 2 Samuel 13:12). It is not mere foolishness but moral outrage.

Beliyya'al, worthlessness or wickedness, often used in the phrase sons of worthlessness for wicked men. Here it describes the men of Gibeah (19:22). In later Jewish writing the word became a name for Satan, and Paul uses it in that sense (2 Corinthians 6:15).

Lev, heart, used in 19:3 when the Levite goes to speak to her heart, and in the father's repeated urging to refresh and gladden the heart. The word suggests the inner life and will. The contrast between the Levite's intention to speak to her heart and his later cold treatment of her is part of the story's tragedy.

christ: This chapter is one of the places where the connection to Christ is most clearly by contrast. The Levite, whose calling was to serve at God's sanctuary, gave his wife to her attackers to save himself. The New Testament calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), a love that suffers for the sake of the other instead of sacrificing the other for its own safety. The broken body sent to the twelve tribes becomes a summons to war and further killing; Christians remember a different body, broken and given for the life of the world, which reconciles rather than divides (1 Corinthians 11:24; Ephesians 2:16). The chapter's unanswered cry for justice for a voiceless victim is also part of the longing that the Bible's story carries forward, to a king who will defend the cause of the poor and the oppressed (Psalm 72:4).

hard.q: Why is such a horrifying story in the Bible, and why does the text seem to say so little in condemnation?
hard.a: The story is in Scripture because it is true to what human beings, including God's people, can become, and because it serves the book's argument. Judges is showing what happens when Israel abandons the LORD and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. The narrator condemns by presentation rather than commentary: the echoes of Sodom, the woman's silence, the image of her hands on the threshold, and the Levite's heartless response speak clearly. Many readers, including feminist scholars, have drawn attention to how the text exposes violence against women by giving attention to the victim's suffering. Others note that the whole nation's shocked response (19:30) and the following war show that Israel itself recognized this as an outrage. Many interpreters also observe that the Levite's own account in chapter 20 conceals his role, which the reader already knows. The absence of a divine voice in the chapter is part of the point: this is Israel without God's rule.

questions: The Levite chose an Israelite town over a foreign one for safety and found none. What does it mean that the greatest danger in this story came from within God's people?
The woman in this story is never named and never speaks. How does the narrative ask the reader to see her, and whom might we overlook in similar ways?
The chapter ends with a call to consider, take counsel, and speak. How should communities of faith respond when terrible wrongs are exposed among them?
